comparison: Both strongly support the characterization of inconsistent literature (C1, C2, C21-C23). OpenEval notes this represents a reasonable synthesis; peer reviewers explicitly praise this framing as 'perfect' and 'precisely why the data is valuable.'

Both support the study's motivation regarding inconsistent results (C3, C4). OpenEval includes these in broader literature synthesis; peer reviewers specifically endorse this as 'important and timely' without challenge.

Both strongly support the experimental design and methodology (C5-C7, C27, C30-C35). OpenEval finds methods comprehensive and internally consistent; peer reviewers praise the 'clearly defined experimental parameters' and 'strong experimental protocol.'

Both support the analytical calibration approach (C36-C38). OpenEval describes it as rigorous statistical practice; peer reviewer 1 explicitly praises 'the comparison of several statistical approaches and simulations' as 'thorough and transparent.'
Perfect agreement on general temporal trends (C39-C41). Both accept these as expected patterns in decision-making tasks; no reviewer challenges these observations.

Both express uncertainty about robustness of rhythmicity effects (C42-C44, C47). OpenEval notes 50% prevalence raises robustness questions; peer reviewers critically note 'many effects have lower than 50% significant samples' and question replicability across labs.

Both uncertain about heterogeneity across experiments (C48-C51). OpenEval notes inconsistency undermines confidence in unified mechanism; peer reviewers state 'variable nature of effects leaves impression that effects are not very robust.'

Both uncertain about frequency-specific patterns (C52-C53). OpenEval acknowledges substantial heterogeneity; peer reviewer 1 questions 'whether there is any systematic pattern' versus 'natural variability.'

Both uncertain about ear-specific rhythmicity (C54-C56). OpenEval questions stability of averaged prevalence data; peer reviewers note 'variable nature of effects in different frequency bands and ears' suggests lack of robustness.
OpenEval uncertain about ear independence (C57-C59) requiring replication; peer reviewers support this finding without direct challenge, acknowledging 'ear-specific effects' as valuable.

Both uncertain about dual-task effects (C60-C67). OpenEval notes weak support with modest prevalence; peer reviewers accept findings but don't specifically dispute the weak effects, consistent with overall robustness concerns.

Both support fixation stability findings (C68-C74). OpenEval describes this as one of the most robust findings with high prevalence; peer reviewers acknowledge investigation of 'motor involvement' without challenge.
Both support pupil null finding (C68-C69). OpenEval and peer reviewers accept this as appropriate negative control without dispute.

Disagreement on experimental control (C75-C76). OpenEval supports the adaptive procedure as appropriate control; peer reviewer 2 raises concerns that adaptive adjustment 'may add variance to the data' and 'potentially contribute to weak perceptual rhythmicity.'

Both uncertain about main conclusions (C8, C77-C79). OpenEval notes evidence against universal rhythmicity based on inconsistency rather than definitive nulls; peer reviewers mixed—editor calls evidence 'solid' but reviewer 3 suggests data 'better interpreted as showing no consistent rhythmic mode effect.'

Both uncertain about mechanistic speculation (C80-C81). OpenEval states speculation 'goes beyond the data'; peer reviewer 3 questions theoretical framework, noting cited papers 'largely based on processing of rhythmic stimuli' while task 'seems better suited to continuous vigilance mode.'

OpenEval supports literature review claims (C12-C20, C24-C29) as fair characterization with appropriate citations. No corresponding specific peer evaluation found, though peer reviewers generally accept the literature framing.

OpenEval supports detailed analytical framework including calibration, simulations, and bootstrapping (C104-C119) as sound statistical practice. While peer reviewer 1 praises the approach generally (R4), no peer evaluation specifically addresses these detailed methodological claims.
